title: Stack, Heap, and Storage Duration
relevance: Interviews and OAs assume you know where data lives, how long it lives, and what breaks when stack or heap rules are violated.

phases.goal: Establish the process address-space layout and how C++ storage durations map onto those segments.

must_hit.point: A running process has distinct regions: text/code, initialised data, BSS, heap growing upward, stack growing downward, plus argv/env at the high end.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks high-to-low or low-to-high consistently and names one example of what lives in each region.

must_hit.point: BSS holds zero-initialised globals/statics so large zeroed arrays cost almost nothing in the executable; the OS maps zero-filled pages at load time.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts BSS with the data segment and mentions the binary-size motivation.

must_hit.point: C++ has four storage durations—automatic, static, dynamic, and thread—that decide when storage is obtained and released.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists all four and maps them: locals→stack, global/static→data or BSS, new/malloc→heap, thread_local→per-thread storage.

must_hit.point: Scope is name visibility; lifetime/storage duration is when the object exists in memory—a static local has narrow scope but program-long lifetime.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates scope from lifetime and uses a static local as the contrasting example.

probes: Describe the memory layout of a running C++ process.
What is the difference between scope and lifetime?

hints.1: Think of the process image as labelled zones, not one shapeless blob of RAM.
hints.2: Name text, data, BSS, heap, and stack, then say which storage duration lands in each.
hints.3: Automatic→stack frame; static→data/BSS for the whole program; dynamic→heap until delete/free; thread_local→one copy per thread.

phases.goal: Explain call-stack frames, why locals vanish on return, and how heap allocation/deallocation works.

must_hit.point: A stack frame holds return address, saved registers, parameters/arguments, locals, and optionally a frame pointer; the stack pointer tracks the current top.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the main frame contents and notes layout is ABI-specific but the idea is shared.

must_hit.point: On return the callee frame is popped, automatic lifetime ends, and returning a pointer or reference to a local is undefined behaviour.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says the frame is gone so the caller holds a dangling address; contrasts with return by value.

must_hit.point: Each recursive call gets its own frame, so recursion consumes stack space proportional to depth.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties deep/infinite recursion to a tall tower of frames and stack exhaustion.

must_hit.point: new pairs with delete and new[] with delete[]; mixing them, or mixing new/malloc with the wrong deallocator, is undefined behaviour.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the matching pairs and that free/delete must not be crossed with the wrong allocator.

probes: Why does returning a local pointer break?
Walk through what happens to the stack when main calls a helper and that helper returns.

hints.1: Picture each call as placing a tray on a cafeteria stack.
hints.2: On call: push frame and move the stack pointer down; on return: pop frame and jump to the saved return address.
hints.3: After return, automatic storage is reusable stack space—the bits may linger, but the object's lifetime has ended, so any pointer into it dangles.

phases.goal: Compare stack and heap on speed, size budget, lifetime, management, and failure modes.

must_hit.point: Stack allocation is essentially a stack-pointer adjust (few instructions, LIFO locality); heap allocation walks allocator metadata, may lock, and can involve syscalls when the arena grows.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts pointer-bump vs free-list/search overhead and mentions possible brk/mmap growth.

must_hit.point: The stack is fast but small—typical defaults are on the order of 1–8 MB per thread—while the heap is limited by available virtual memory/RAM.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites the 1–8 MB order of magnitude and notes Windows often 1 MB and many Linux setups 8 MB.

must_hit.point: Heap fragmentation can leave enough free bytes in aggregate with no contiguous block large enough; the stack's LIFO discipline makes fragmentation inapplicable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names external vs internal fragmentation and contrasts with stack LIFO.

must_hit.point: Characteristic failure modes differ: stack overflow vs leaks, dangling pointers, double free, and bad_alloc/nullptr from heap allocation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Pairs stack overflow with recursion/huge locals, and heap failures with leak/dangling/double-free/bad_alloc.

probes: Why is heap allocation slower than stack allocation?

hints.1: Lead with lifetime and who manages the memory, then size and speed.
hints.2: Use the decision criteria: speed, size budget, lifetime, manager, failure mode, fragmentation.
hints.3: Stack: automatic locals, pointer bump, ~1–8 MB, overflow; heap: new/malloc until free, allocator overhead, large budget, leaks/fragmentation.

phases.goal: Apply layout and lifetime rules to overflow avoidance, object placement, and safe ownership.

must_hit.point: A huge automatic array (for example int a[10'000'000]) is a stack allocation and can overflow; prefer heap-backed std::vector, or a static/global buffer in BSS for large scratch arrays.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Identifies the local giant array as stack, not heap, and names vector or static/global as mitigations.

must_hit.point: For MyClass* p = new MyClass(), members live inside the heap object; p itself is typically an automatic pointer on the stack.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates the pointer's storage from the object's contiguous heap block (members, padding, vptr if any).

must_hit.point: sizeof includes padding for alignment, so member order can change size; reordering by decreasing alignment often shrinks sizeof.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains padding for alignment and that two structs with the same members can differ in size by order.

must_hit.point: Prefer RAII and smart pointers (unique_ptr/shared_ptr) or vector over raw new/delete so cleanup survives early returns and exceptions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties acquire-in-ctor/release-in-dtor to automatic cleanup and names the modern tools.

probes: What causes a stack overflow, and how do you fix it in competitive programming?
If I have MyClass* p = new MyClass();, where are the members?

hints.1: Ask whether the big data is a local, a global/static, or a new/vector allocation.
hints.2: Overflow staples: deep recursion and enormous automatic objects; move bulk data off the stack.
hints.3: Rewrite recursion iteratively or raise stack if allowed; put large buffers in vector/new or BSS; remember members live with the enclosing object, not with the pointer variable.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Stack is a near-free pointer bump with LIFO locality but a small fixed budget and lifetime tied to the frame; heap supports large/long-lived data via the allocator but pays metadata, possible locks/syscalls, poorer locality, and fragmentation risk.

tradeoffs.topic: Deep recursion vs iterative / heap-backed approach
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Call recursion uses stack proportional to depth and can overflow on deep graphs; an explicit std::stack/loop or heap/static buffers moves frames or bulk data off the limited stack. Do not rely on tail-call optimisation in C++—it is not guaranteed.

tradeoffs.topic: Raw new/delete vs RAII smart pointers
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Manual pairing fails under early returns and exceptions; RAII ties release to destructors, and unique_ptr/shared_ptr (or vector for arrays) are preferred in application code while raw owning pointers remain mainly an interview topic.

tradeoffs.topic: Giant local array vs vector vs static/global buffer
tradeoffs.strong_answer: A large automatic array competes for the few megabytes of stack; std::vector puts payload on the heap; a global/static array lands in data/BSS—three segment choices for the same logical scratch data.

gotchas.trap: Returning a pointer or reference to a function-local automatic variable.
gotchas.correction: The callee frame is popped and lifetime ends; return by value, or point to longer-lived storage (static, caller-owned, or heap via smart pointer).

gotchas.trap: Treating int a[10000000]; inside a function as a heap allocation.
gotchas.correction: It is automatic stack storage; use std::vector, new, or a static/global BSS buffer for huge sizes.

gotchas.trap: Mixing new with delete[], new[] with delete, free with new, or delete with malloc.
gotchas.correction: Match new↔delete, new[]↔delete[], malloc↔free; mismatches are undefined behaviour.

gotchas.trap: Double-deleting or leaving a non-null pointer after delete.
gotchas.correction: Deleting twice is UB and can corrupt allocator metadata; set the pointer to nullptr defensively after delete.

gotchas.trap: Relying on initialisation order across different static objects in different translation units.
gotchas.correction: That is the static initialisation order fiasco; avoid subtle cross-TU static ordering dependencies.

gotchas.trap: Assuming members accessed through a stack pointer live on the stack.
gotchas.correction: Members live wherever the enclosing object lives—inside the heap block for a new'd object, even if the pointer variable is automatic.
